utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I must apologise for the delay. One Judge, as you can see, has been detained and so Judge Thelin and I will sit under Rule 15 bis, and we hope to receive news in the course of the morning. The witness is being brought in, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit me to address you while we're waiting for the witness, just so that we can save time. I'm going to do everything possible to finish with this witness today, because new witnesses are arriving, so we do not want to then have this witness stay over until next week. Our witnesses are also military officials, and they also are obliged to return to their duties. There are certain restrictions regarding their stay abroad. This is why I am telling you this, and I would like to ask my learned friend from the Prosecution to keep this in mind during cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I just apologise again that we've lost you some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Shutters. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. You're going to testify here under protective measures. You have been given a pseudonym. I'm going to address you during the examination-in-chief as "sir." You will have voice and face distortion. A court officer now is going to show you a piece of paper for you to go over your particulars, and then you can say aloud that these are your particulars and that they are correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the document to the other parties in the proceedings and the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, I would like to tender this as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 793, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in order to complete your testimony today, all the parties are going to do their utmost that that is so, so that you could leave to go back home tomorrow and so that you do not have to stay here during the weekend. And for that reason, I would like to ask that your answers to me or to the other side be as brief and as concise as possible. I would also like to ask you to make a pause between my question and your answer so that your answer could be recorded correctly in the transcript, the way you said it. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would also warn you that at certain points we're going to move into private session, which means that the session will be not broadcast in public and those parts during private session will not be part of the public transcript. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now move into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us whether the Prosecution ever requested an interview with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you actually had this interview; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I was summoned to come on the 15th of September at 2.00 p.m., which is what I did. I responded to the request for the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a waiver from keeping military secrets during the interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, as you are testifying before this Trial Chamber, have you been given this waiver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence received a recording of that interview that you had with the Prosecutor's office. Can you please tell us how long the interview lasted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: About an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was the microphone switched on during the entire interview that you had with the representatives of the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what your response was to the request by the Prosecution to interview you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I warned them that I did not have the waiver relating to military secrets.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did they say when they heard your answer? What kind of a statement did they ask for?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received an initial 65 ter summary on July 11th, indicating four items that this witness was going to testify to. We received a second supplemental summary on July 31st as to what this witness was going to testify to. Yesterday we received something - I'm not sure what this is - called proofing notes, I have copies for the Court, listing about another ten items that this witness is going to speak about. This is not on any list of what this witness is going to speak about. Those proofing notes are so general you can state what the witness is going to speak about, any specific facts. I didn't listen to that tape yesterday. I would have if I knew this issue was going to be raised. From the proofing notes, it is clear we have no idea, in many important areas, what this witness is going to say. We have no advance notice. I spoke with Ms. Tapuskovic yesterday. I got some information in some of these areas, but on certain areas, such as Seselj's visit to Vukovar, it's going to be interesting because we have no idea what this witness is going to say. On Radic's relationship with other soldiers in neighbouring units, no idea what this witness is going to say. With regard to this issue, we have no idea what this witness is going to say because we have had no notice of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what my colleague Mr. Weiner says is only partially correct. When the 65 ter list was drafted and when the brief summaries were handed over, the witness still did not have the waiver from keeping military secrets. So he did agree, in principle, to testify and, in principle, he just gave us brief indications what he would testify about. The witness was waived from keeping military secrets. On one of those days when I addressed the Trial Chamber, that was when the Defence was actually here in The Hague and we were unable to actually speak with the witness in detail. A detailed conversation with the witness was conducted only when the witness came to The Hague and when we proofed this witness, and that is when we made the notes. That day we were in court until 4.00 p.m., and we were only able to speak with the witness from 6.00 p.m. onwards. And then the next day we, of course, had to come back to the courtroom. According to the 65 ter documents, based on how the Defence understand them, it is actually testimony of the witness relating to certain counts of the indictment. What I asked the witness now does not refer to the indictment, but it refers to actually what the witness requested yesterday when I went to see him and when I informed him that he would testify a little bit later and that he would also need to talk about how the Prosecution had the interview with him in Belgrade and why he refused to provide a statement to the Prosecution, because my learned friend Mr. Moore announced here yesterday that the witness had changed his position, but he didn't provide any further information. So the witness would like to explain why he said, during the interview in Belgrade, that he was prepared to speak with them again and why he said yesterday that he did not wish to speak with them. So if the Trial Chamber believes that this is not relevant, then I am going to move on to my next point in the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, the position of the witness in speaking to or not speaking to either party before the witness comes to give evidence is not, at the outset, a matter of relevance to this Chamber. If he has cross-examined on the basis that the witness has changed his position from what he said, then it does become of relevance. So at the moment you have no need to go into this, and in view of the position and objection of Mr. Weiner, I doubt that he will be doing so himself. The second matter raised is whether, for example, this last note is an adequate indication of the facts on which the witness will testify. That is what the rule requires, that the summaries of evidence identify the facts as to which the witness will testify. Now, that, of course, means the important and significant facts, not every possible detail, because it's not a full statement; it's merely a summary. But the document that is here merely, at the most, identifies a topic and does not identify what are the facts about which the witness will testify. It may be, therefore, that once he has given evidence, it may become necessary for the Prosecution to seek an adjournment before they cross-examine. I don't know whether that will occur and I hope it doesn't. But that's the consequence of an outline of evidence which fails to identify adequately the material facts about which the witness will testify. So at the moment you will be free, of course, to proceed with your evidence. There's no need to deal with the question of whether or not the witness spoke to the Prosecution. And we will hope that it proves possible in the course of the day for Mr. Weiner to be able to conduct and complete his cross-examination. Just at this moment, the Judges will rise for a minute, and I'm pleased to say we'll be able to continue with three Judges. --- Break taken at 9.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us whether you know the accused, Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us since when you've known him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Since November 1990, when I came to the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you went to the Vukovar front with Mr. Radic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please move into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us if you took part in the combat actions of your company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When your colleagues were in combat, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I was at the company stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the address of these company stations where you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I really couldn't give you the number. One of them was in Svetozara Markovica Street and the other one was in Nova Ulica Street, at our observation post.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us in whose house the observation post was located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: In the house of a certain Stanko.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me why this house was chosen as the observation post, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Because it was a very solidly built house, it had more than one storey, and the company commander was able to have a good overview of the terrain from the roof of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you use that house until the end of your stay in Vukovar as an observation post? Did you stay in that house until the end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: There were several observation posts, but this observation post was the one where we spent most of our time. But there were several observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that this house, this observation post that you mentioned, was safe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us where you slept during your stay in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: At the observation post and at the other company station from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see on our screens a Defence exhibit, 2D11, that is, -0169.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, does this sketch say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: That is our observation post.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that is the house where you slept, as you said a few moments ago; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the usher to give the witness a pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to ask you to use this pen on the screen where you see the photograph, to show us things or perhaps draw things for us, and what you draw will remain in the form of a red line. Sir, can you draw for us on this sketch of the observation post where it was that you slept, as you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that with a number 1 on the side, and could you circle that number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you know where Captain Radic slept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you place a number 2 within that circle. And could you please respond by speaking into the microphone so that we have your answer recorded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: This is where Captain Radic slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what number you used to mark the place where Captain Radic had slept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you remember whether anybody else slept in this house, in addition to the two of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: A soldier, Dejan Petkovic. Petkovic. I don't remember the names exactly. I would not want the Court to misunderstand me. There was this one soldier who was a Muslim, but I do not recall his name. And from time to time, a journalist, or rather, a war reporter, Peternek.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us just where they slept, in which house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: In this same house where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what numbers 3, 7, 6, and 5 denote on this sketch.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Could I please have a look. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what they denote.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: That is a low building, if I can put it that way, which was close to the street, that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was in that low building, what you or anybody else from your company did in that building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: On this picture, the number 5 shows where the company office was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what a company office is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: A place where the company commander studied the assignments he got from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you one more thing. Could you please draw something for us, namely in what room others, that is to say, either soldiers or other visitors that you mentioned a few moments ago, slept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: As for the persons I mentioned, well, yes. But as far as I know, there were no visitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Peternek. He was not a soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, he was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, then, where Peternek and the other soldiers you mentioned slept. Can you mark this for us on this sketch.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take the pen and actually draw it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what is this that you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Places where the said persons slept, and Mr. Peternek, from time to time, when he was staying with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number 794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have kept the sketch from before, Your Honours, so that it wouldn't get lost. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us whether what you drew were beds, or did people sleep there in some other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: People slept in other places as well, but what I drew here, number 2 was a bed. As for the rest, it was makeshift; blankets, sleeping bags, and people slept on the floor, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, do you know up until when your company had a combat task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Up until the 9th or 10th of November. I think it was the 10th, all things considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On what is your memory based? How come you are saying it's the 9th or the 10th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Because that was the end of combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me for whom this was the end of combat actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Our 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the combat task was that your company had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Our company had the task of deblocking and liberating the barracks from formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you what exactly the task of your company was, the company that you belonged to, your company. Can you tell me on what axis your company was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. Nova Ulica-Milovo Brdo was the axis.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, after the 10th, where was your company staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: At the observation posts, or rather, at the observation post and at the places where the army had been grouped. As for Milovo Brdo, we had part of our people there for the purpose of security and for the purpose of guarding these positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for all these days, from the 10th, where did you bring food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, an objection, just for the record. We are well outside of the notice provided to the Prosecution, any of these three notices. All we have is the combat task of his unit and when it was accomplished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the second one is his activities up to the moment of departure from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to the last note that was submitted to the Prosecution, that was yesterday, early in the morning, it says that the witness will explain what the combat tasks of his company were, when the combat task was accomplished, and his activities from that moment all the way up to his departure for Belgrade. So I think that the Defence did provide a frame for what the witness would be speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're not going to spend time on this now, Ms. Tapuskovic, but could I point out that's precisely the problem. You have indicated in this "subject matters about which the witness will give evidence," you have not identified the material facts about which he will speak. And that's the difference. But as I indicated earlier, we won't delay now. If you could carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us -- or rather, I put a question to you before my colleague Mr. Weiner objected. The question was where you took food to the soldiers from your company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Specifically for these soldiers who were at that particular line of security, that is where I brought food. As for the others, to the company station.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, can you remember what it was that you did on the 18th of November; and if you can remember, can you tell us how it is that you remember that that happened on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: On the 18th we had our regular assignments. As a matter of fact, I was the busiest on that day because of the materiel that had to be collected; however, in the afternoon we received information that combat activity has been completed in Vukovar, that it was over.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember what else you did on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, I went to Negoslavci to take some equipment, or rather, shirts, uniforms that were being laundered, so that our soldiers could get clean ones, and I took about ten uniforms that had come to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall repeat the question in part because of the mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the uniforms that you took. How many did you take and how many arrived in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I took my equipment, the one that I had handed over, or rather, the clothes that I handed over to be laundered, and I took one camouflage uniform. I think that ten had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether these uniforms that had arrived were new uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. The one that I picked up was new. The rest of the things that I picked up were actually items that had been laundered and repaired.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us now if you remember what happened then. Can you describe what you did the next day, the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. The next day there were some activities relating to preparation of food, delivery of food. We were also given an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what assignment you were given that day, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: In the morning, I don't know exactly when, Captain Radic received an assignment from the battalion commander to go across the Vuka River, across the bridge, with other soldiers to the hospital, and to secure the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us the name of your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: The battalion commander was Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you saw or heard when the order was issued to Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. I was very close when the order came through the radio for this assignment that I mentioned to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, what sort of radio device was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what kind it was, but it was some sort of Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who had the Motorolas in your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: There were two in our company; one was with Captain Radic and the other one was with Lieutenant (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, was there a reason why (redacted), in particular, had the Motorola as opposed to any of the other soldiers in the company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. First, Lieutenant (redacted) was the deputy commander of the company. Another important reason why he had the Motorola was because he was further away from Captain Radic and from our positions because of the kind of assignment he was given, and they had to be in contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you were given the assignment, can you briefly describe what happened then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: When we were given the assignment, or rather, when Captain Radic was given the assignment, I was there. There were some 15 or 20 soldiers there, too, and we were supposed to carry out this order. Should I finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you can remember any of the soldiers, their names, who set off on this assignment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, up to a point. (redacted), Miro Lepojevic, and as for the rest, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me how you came from Milovo Brdo to your destination in order to carry out the assignment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: We took a couple of cars, without any preparation or an assessment of the situation, and set off in the direction of the hospital. There were four or five cars, actually, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to the hospital from Milovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: From the moment we set off, perhaps it took 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you did once you reached the hospital, you and the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: When we got to the hospital, Captain Radic ordered us to take up positions around the hospital, to secure the hospital, not to allow anyone to enter or to leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how long you secured the hospital? How long did this last in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I don't know how many hours we were there, but we were there until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the soldiers were doing during that time that they were securing the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: We were given an assignment, and then each of us were given a sector that we were supposed to monitor. I went with soldier (redacted) and two or three others - I don't know their names - to secure the left side of the hospital as you're looking in the direction of the MUP. When we came to that part, it was noticed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause there. Thank you. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but certain names have been said; one is page 19, line 25, and the other is page 20, line 21. I was going to wait until the end but it's continuing. If certain names are going to be used, could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've been signing redactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you continue now, please. These were just some procedural matters. You can continue. My question was: What happened then, and how did you carry out your assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. I'm speaking about me and the men who were with me. On the left side of the hospital, looking in the direction of the MUP and the municipal building, we took up positions there. Soldier (redacted) noted two containers with, let's say, strange contents. We, or rather, I went up there. (redacted) looked through the contents of those bags. There were uniforms in those bags. I specifically told him, "Please leave that. I don't want to be looking at all kinds of things." He continued to take out these bags, and he warned me that these were uniforms. And I saw that for myself afterwards, that these were uniforms. They were in good condition. There were no holes from bullets. I assumed that these were uniforms from the wounded, but no, these were in good condition. They were a little bit dirty, perhaps, but there was no trace of blood. So this was complete equipment. At the time when Borovo was working, the Borovo factory, they used to make these boots, yellow boots. They were also in good conditions. And the boots were called Kanadjanke, Canadian boots. But we found 10 to 15 black uniforms in good condition, with insignia on the left and the right side of the sleeves. There was a letter U as well as insignia with HOS, indicating the Croatian defence forces. There were a number of camouflage uniforms of American manufacture. I don't know that I am exaggerating. We recognised them because they had special kind of bomber jackets; we call them Vijetnamka. And there were also some Velcro fastenings, indicating that these were uniforms belonging to some formations. There were also plenty of green M-77 uniforms; that's what they were called at the time. Anyone had that uniform at that time at home. This was pursuant to the laws that were in force at that time. Everybody had to have a uniform at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. I was waiting for you to pause because our voices mustn't overlap. But anyway, what did it mean to you when you saw those uniforms with the U and the HOS insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: As a professional, the first thing that came to mind was that these were enemy formations' uniforms, uniforms from people from the other side, who had taken them off and who were concealing themselves, hiding somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like us now to look at Exhibit 170 on the monitors. This is a set of photographs. Can we please look at a photograph that is third in order, and it bears the number 0053-1258. It's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If there are any problems, while we're waiting for the picture on the screen, I'm going to put my question to you, sir, so that we can save time. What did you do when you saw those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, since I am a professional, the first thing that came to mind was that someone had taken off those uniforms and that perhaps these people are somewhere nearby, that we had encountered an ambush. So I went to look for Captain Radic to inform him about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now you can see on the screen in front of you a photograph. Can you tell what you see in this photograph. Do you recognise what is on this photograph? On the right-hand monitor, can you see what's there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was just waiting for the interpretation to finish. Yes, that's the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "that's the hospital," you mean the Vukovar Hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you take the marker again, please, and indicate on the photograph the places where you and the other soldiers from your company were deployed. Can you point on the photograph to the place where you saw that container. When you indicate the container, can you please mark that with number 1, and can you mark the other points accordingly, and then we will know that these were the places where the soldiers were deployed. Can you please do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No, I cannot indicate that here because we were not -- actually, I and my soldiers were not on this side.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. We're going to look for other photographs. This is another photograph, the fourth in order, and the number is 1259. Sir, does this jog your memory, this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Up to a point. Actually, if you do have the photograph, what I need is this side here, the side facing the direction of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about this side of the hospital and the picture you can see now? Does that jog your memory in terms of the place where you were, where you secured the hospital? Can you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, that is my sector. That's the sector that I was securing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now indicate, can you now draw what I asked you to, namely, the place where you saw the container with these uniforms, and can you mark that with number 1; as well as the places where you and the others, the other soldiers, if you recall as far as the other soldiers are concerned, or rather, where you were deployed in order to secure the hospital. Could you please take the marker and try to draw this for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, this is where the container were, a small one here and a big one here, here, and here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So let's mark these squares, if we are going to call them that, 1 and 2. Could you put the numbers 1 and 2 within those squares, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, those are containers, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now draw -- we just have two minutes left until the break. Can you draw exactly where it was that the soldiers were standing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: We were not on the tree; we were underneath the tree.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now to mark those circles with capital letters A, B, C, and D next to the circles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now whether Captain Radic was at any one of these places, A, B, C, or D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this drawing made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, I told the witness that we would be having a break now, but we started with a bit of a delay, so I don't know whether we are actually taking the break now or whether I should go on for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said to us before you drew this that you wanted to find Captain Radic; right? I'm just repeating what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to find him and I found Captain Radic. I wanted to report to him about what we had found.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, where did you find Captain Radic and what was his answer to what you said, namely what you had found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I found Captain Radic -- well, on the other side of the hospital. He was somewhere around there. Now, I cannot show the place to you exactly, but it was on the other side of the hospital that I found him and that I informed him about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did he answer to you when you informed him about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: He didn't give me any kind of answer. He just ran after me. I don't know whether you can see this. He ran, say, from the back side of the hospital towards me, and along the way he told all the soldiers on the way, "Maximum combat alert, prepare for action," because that was the only thing that we could expect. And together with me, he came to this place, 1 and 2, to see what this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you -- or rather, I would like to ask the usher to show photograph number 3 from the same set. Sir, do you see this photograph? It is the side opposite to the one that you were showing us a moment ago. It's not on the side, but it is the exact opposite. Can you draw a circle around the place where you came across Captain Radic, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, that's the side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you use an arrow to mark the direction in which, as you said, Captain Radic started moving after you told him what you told him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. After I informed him about this, after I informed Captain Radic about this, in this area where the soldiers were, he immediately told them, "Maximum combat alert. Get ready. We can be attacked. We don't know where from." As a matter of fact, we were even expecting to be attacked from the hospital. And together with me he set out in this direction. Along the way he was telling other people -- I don't know whether there's an entrance into the hospital here, too. But then we went around and came to this place where I had been before. Here, you can see it, where these containers were. You can see it here. I'll do it this way because it's a small photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to use a circle to indicate where Captain Radic had set out from, using a capital A, and then could you please mark the second circle with a capital B and could you draw the arrow a bit more clearly so that we can see even later that that is the direction in which you were moving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark this other circle with a B. As far as I managed to hear you, you said that these were containers. You can put a circle underneath, or rather, next to the circle you can put a number a letter B.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And since you said that already at point A Captain Radic said to the soldiers, "Full combat alert, full combat readiness," can you tell us where the soldiers were standing? Can you indicate that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: This side -- I'm not sure where people were standing exactly. I don't want it to seem that there were too few of us or too many of us, so I'm doing it tentatively. Say 5 or 10 metres was the distance between individual soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please place numbers next to every one of these little circles so that we would know later what these little circles denote.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Is this what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. So basically this is what they were -- this is where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this photograph please be admitted into evidence into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 796, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now what happened then, after you had informed Captain Radic about what you had found in front of the hospital, rather, within the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I omitted to mention one thing a few moments ago. When I started looking for Captain Radic - over here is where the entrance was, I thought that Captain Radic was there, perhaps. I went in; I went out. He was not there, and I continued moving along all the way up to Captain Radic, where I actually found him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could other microphones please be switched off in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly where this other hall was where you came? And can you tell us what number was placed so that we would understand what you mean by this subcorridor; that's the word that you used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I put a Roman numeral VII and VIII, so the subcorridor can be seen exactly. It is going underneath the ground. I'm trying to say that it is an underground thing. And there is also something above it which I don't know, I mean I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me approximately whether you remember when that security was put in place on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I've just said that I cannot remember exactly, but it was in the afternoon. Let's say in the late afternoon hours, that is to say, that it was not dark yet. That is how long we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the soldiers that took part in securing the hospital, who set out together with you and Radic towards the hospital, were all of them soldiers who were members of your unit, that is to say, the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were active soldiers. And I and Captain Radic and Lieutenant Hadzic, the three of us were active-duty officers and active soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now conclude on this subject: Can you tell us how you completed this task of securing the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Since Captain Radic left the sector of the hospital a bit earlier, Lieutenant Hadzic took us out and handed over the security of the hospital to the military police of our guards battalion so that they would go on securing the facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who appeared on behalf of the military police when this handover of security took place? Who commanded that military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Should I say so, or do we have to do that in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I think it was Captain Simic. I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be a convenient moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we must have a half-hour break because of the redactions. You'll have to be very conscious of time, Ms. Tapuskovic. We will resume at 20 minutes past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that you found uniforms which had been discarded within the perimeter of the hospital. Can you tell us whether you found anything else within the hospital perimeter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, and I would kindly ask you if you could again show me the picture of the positions where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see a need for that. We will abide by the order of the Trial Chamber that your examination should be over as soon as possible. You don't have to point to where you found things, but just tell us whether you found something, and what.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: We found weapons, pistols, hunting rifles, rifles, PAM guns, shotguns.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, whom did you see in front of the hospital? Was there anybody else in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. Later on our battalion commander came.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me what you did when you handed the security over to Simic; isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I just said that Captain Radic left the area somewhat earlier. Lieutenant Hadzic was in charge of us because he was the deputy commander of the company. Lieutenant Hadzic handed over the hospital and the security of the hospital to the military police company. And we ourselves went to the observation point.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please remember what happened that evening at the observation point, and who spent the night at the observation point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: On our return to the observation point, which was later that afternoon, I personally handed over the uniform to Captain Radic. That's the uniform that I had worn the previous day, and it was a camouflage uniform. I previously took it from Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a correction in the transcript, where it says that the witness had worn the uniform on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain whether you brought the camouflage uniform, and who you handed this uniform over to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes. On the previous day I brought the uniform from Negoslavci, and on that evening I handed it over to Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe that uniform and how many parts it consisted of. Just a brief description, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: It was a camouflage uniform from the first series of those uniforms that were made. As far as I remember, there was a pair of trousers, a shirt, an anorak and a hat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: It was a camouflage hat. And the shape was a Tito's hat, which was part of the M-77 uniform previously, our uniform, but the colour was different, it was a camouflage colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the second part of my previous question? Can you please remember where you spent the night, where Radic spent the night, and where other soldiers from your company spent that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I remained in the house, at the observation point that is, and all the soldiers were grouped into three houses across the road from the battalion command. Those were three terraced [Realtime transcript read in error "terrorist"] houses, and in one of them was my company station. All the soldiers were there, in groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 33, in line 1, it says those were "terrorist" houses, which has in the meantime been corrected into three houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please tell us where Captain Radic spent that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: You mean the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I believe that he was also in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned three houses in that street, in the vicinity of the battalion command. I am now asking you: In which house did Captain Radic spend that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: He spent that night in the second house, in the middle of that terrace. There were three houses in the terrace and he was sleeping in the middle house on that night, during that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened the following day, the 20th of November? Can you remember where people were and what your activities were on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, I had a lot of things to do in terms of bringing over materiel and dealing and looking after that, and that lasted into the late afternoon hours of that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened in the evening hours? Where was Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There has never been any notice to anything happening in relation to this witness on the 20th, be it the initial notes of -- the initial 65 ter of July 11th, the second 65 ter or the updates on the 31st, and even the so-called proofing notes. And at this point I have no idea where this is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the proofing note that was provided to the Prosecutor is what it is, and obviously the Prosecutor is not happy with those proofing notes. However, we did indicate that the witness would testify in general terms about what he did from the fall of Vukovar to the moment when his company, i.e., the entire brigade, left to go to Belgrade. I'm going to rephrase my question and I'll ask the witness what he did on the following day, whom he saw on the following day, and how he contacted his men, his troops, the troops from his company, on the following day, in the course of the 20th of November, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is getting beyond what is any attempt to provide what is required by the Rules, Ms. Tapuskovic. I have looked down this proofing note again, and there is absolutely no hint that this topic will even be touched on. There's certainly no indication of the material facts about which the witness will speak. There are two courses open to the Chamber: One, we could refuse to allow the evidence to be led; the other is allow it to be led, but if the Prosecution is genuinely embarrassed by it, to have to adjourn then to allow them to prepare their cross-examination. The consequence of that is to get you into difficulty with your witness because of the basis that he is here and the time that he is allowed to be here by his army.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a member of Mr. Radic's team, I accept your suggestions and I accept your criticism about our proofing notes. And we are entirely in your hands and we shall abide by your decision, whether to continue this witness's testimony about the circumstances or whether to leave the Prosecutor time to prepare for the cross-examination that would cover this new area of examination. I can also withdraw any questions about that day. I'm withdrawing all my future questions about that day to save time and to be able to draw this witness's testimony to an end. I will, therefore, move on to another topic. Let me just tell you that the topic of the 20th of November has to do with the item of the proofing notes which reads "the order was conveyed to him to line up the troops on the 21st of November." But if you wish me to do so, I will move on immediately to the 21st of November, without dealing with the process of the order having been conveyed to him on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that would be an excellent course to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what happened on the 21st of November, in the early morning hours. What were your activities on that day? Whom did you see and whom did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Before that, I would like to say something, if I may. I can see that the 20th of November is in dispute. In the questions that I received from the Prosecutor, I was waived from keeping the military secret and I can talk about the 20th and the 21st as per their request.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the express order by the Trial Chamber, we skipped the questions by the Prosecutor and the information that they wanted to elicit from you; that's why I'm asking you to answer my question. And the question was: What you did on the 21st; if you remember, why you remember this; and whom did you see on that day, and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: On the 21st of November, I got up somewhat earlier because I was at the observation point. I looked around and Captain Radic was not there. I went out of that house, and in the adjacent building I found Captain Radic asleep there. I woke him up, and then we embarked on the preparations for the lining up of the troops. This had been ordered by the battalion command. The review took place in front of the observation point in Nova Street. Captain Stijakovic carried out the review of the troops. The troops returned to their positions in the area of deployment. Captain Radic was very tired. He said, "I'm going to have some rest." He returned to rest. I was there as well, because that was one part of my company's station. That's where I prepared the ammunition. I sealed the boxes to prevent looting. And the whole day actually reduced to the preparations for the return to Belgrade, which had been ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you who you saw, who you met that day, but we can go back to the review. Can you please tell us how long the review lasted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I cannot really say how many minutes it lasted, but Captain Radic reported to Captain Stijakovic. Captain Stijakovic reviewed the unit, inspected the unit, greeted them; we greeted him in turn. We saluted him. There was an inspection of the soldiers, whether everything was in order, whether the soldiers were shaved, and so on. He was there for a couple of minutes more, and then he continued on with his regular duties. So the only person I saw was Captain Stijakovic; no one else was there at that review except us soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you remember what else you did that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: We continued with our preparations for our return. Specifically, in relation to Captain Radic, I know that he was resting at the observation post where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you met anyone else that day outside of the observation post or at the company stations. Who did you meet that day? Who were the people coming to the observation post, if anyone did come to the observation post that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: There was no one at the observation post; no one came either. While I was in this first location where the 1st Company station was, I saw the company commander. There were people who were coming there from the command and so on. I don't know exactly what they were doing there. This was in Svetozara Markovica Street, where the battalion command was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to this. There's been no proper foundation laid as to where he was, what times he was at that observation post, when he was at that observation post. And he says, "No people came when I was there." When is he talking about? Is he talking about the morning, the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not a basis for objection, Mr. Weiner. It's an imprecision that you can correct in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, no proper foundation has been laid, so I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He said he was there at times, and he says, "No one was there when I was there." What's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. As the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It might be that he was only there for ten minutes in the whole day, but there was no one there when he was there. We don't know. But it's not evidence that can be ruled out. It's unclear, and I'm sure now Ms. Tapuskovic will clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've heard the Judge's comment about this particular matter. So, if anybody did come, can you tell us whether they were military officers or members of some other structures. Can you be specific as to who came to the observation post that day after the review?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No one came to the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the 21st, sir, the day of the review.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Other than Captain Stijakovic, who actually conducted the review, no one else came.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. You said that day -- over those few days you were very busy with preparations for your departure to Belgrade. Can you please tell us, if you recall, how much time did you actually spend at the observation post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: The 21st, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the 21st.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I spent more time there than at the other observation post, because the other observation post was where the soldiers were, whereas the other part, this observation post where the company station was, was where I spent most of my time because that's where the ammunition was. And I simply wasn't in a position to leave the place for longer than five to ten minutes because the security conditions were inadequate for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to move to another topic. Can you please tell us what you know about the visit of Vojislav Seselj to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: From what I know, he did come to Vukovar. I don't know exactly the date. Perhaps it was in late October. He passed through Nova Ulica Street, which was close to where I was. And I can say that his guerillas, as they're popularly known, his security guards literally pushed me back into the rooms behind the gates so that I wouldn't be near. Regardless of the fact they saw that I was an active officer, they continued moving along Nova Ulica Street towards the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Vojislav Seselj, you mentioned guerillas. What does that mean when you use that term, "guerillas"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Well, I used that symbolically. What I mean is his close guards, his body-guards, Seselj's body-guards. Our battalion commander was with him also.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if they stayed for any amount of time in front of your observation post.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No, no. They just passed by.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if Captain Miroslav Radic was at the observation post at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No. Captain Radic was out on activities, at an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me now, who were the soldiers under the command of Captain Radic, or which soldiers were under the command of Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Captain Radic was in command of the 3rd Company of the 1st Motorised Battalion of the JNA, the units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he communicated only with the members of his company at the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before he answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Again, we're outside -- we're outside of any notice to us on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: About what, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On who the members of Captain Radic's company were, his communications with people. I'm not sure where this is heading, but it seems to be outside the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Ms. Tapuskovic, but Mr. Weiner is foreshadowing he may well not be able to cross-examine on these topics. We'll have to deal with that should it arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We thought that the proofing notes on page 2, Radic's relationship or attitude towards other soldiers and other units, provides sufficient information to indicate the direction of the examination of this witness, because the definitions were already given and the terms "neighbouring units" and "soldiers" have been described. So that is why we believe that certain things have already been defined on the basis of today's work so that we don't need to provide so many details. But, of course, I accept your position. I'm going to be finished, Your Honours, in about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us, in cases when Captain Radic was not at the command post, when he was absent for some reason, who substituted for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When Captain Radic, for any reason, was not at the observation post, who stood in for him? Who did he authorise to carry out his duties? Who was his deputy for most of the jobs that he was performing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: You mentioned one thing, and this is why I wanted you to repeat the question. Actually, he was replaced by Captain Hadzic, but there was another term that was used and this is why I wanted you to repeat what you asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would like to go back to your activities, something that we discussed at the very beginning of your testimony, and what was your activity. We're not going to repeat that and there's no need to go into private session for that. But the question is: When you were performing your duties, do you know who actually supplied and did the logistics part of the work for units of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: The TO units were supplied from their own sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which TO units were there, that you know of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I know the 1st, 2nd, and the 3rd Companies of the TO were there and the Leva Supoderica Detachment, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who was commanding those units? Can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: The 3rd Company commander was Miroljub Vujanovic, but please, I could be wrong about the surname; so Miroljub Vujanovic. Stanko Vujanovic was also a company commander. As for the Leva Supoderica Detachment, I think it was Milan Lancuzanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it one of your duties, or rather, were you ever told that it would be good also to care for the civilian population? Are you aware of anything like that as being part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: What sort of care or help do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point, or your company help the civilian population in Vukovar? Did you distribute food or did you distribute anything else to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, we did help the civilian population as much as we were able to. It was an individual thing in terms of what we helped them with, what we were able to help them with.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example, at least one example, of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: For example, a couple of times when we could we gave them cans of food. Not much, but whatever it was that we had, we would help them to survive, so that they could have something to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And even the small amount of assistance that you were able to provide, did you provide that without paying any attention to any differences between the citizens, regardless of whether they belonged to one ethnic group or the other? Were there any criteria on the basis of which you provided this assistance; and if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: There were no criteria for that. We were the Yugoslav People's Army, and it was our duty, if we were able to, to help all the people specifically. There were all sorts of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to another topic now and that has to do with Captain Radic's relationship with soldiers and other units. Can you tell me whether, at the observation post, Captain Radic, in any way, in those situations when you were there, did he have encounters of any kind; and if so, with who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No, he did not meet with anyone and no one came to us. Perhaps somebody would come for a few minutes, in passing. But that somebody would get into the observation post itself, the building itself, no. I just know that this certain Stanko was there a few times - I mean, he simply came there because it was his house - and nobody else. And he'd only go to the garden, have a look, turn around, go away.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you mentioned to us that someone was there from the outside. You said that a journalist was there, Peternek. Tell us about this journalist Peternek. How come he was in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Since Mr. Peternek was a legal and official war reporter -- now, I don't know whether he's a journalist or a photo reporter. He was assigned to be at that axis. Now, why he slept where we were, somebody else probably decided about that. But this Mr. Peternek very rarely slept at the observation post. When he was there, as far as I know, for the most part, he was at this house that was across the street from the battalion command, in the street of Svetozara Markovica. I cannot remember exactly, but that's where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether any other journalist showed up there and entered the observation post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No, no. Just Mr. Peternek.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. Mr. Domazet, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some questions, but there might be some issues that I might request until Monday, based on some of the testimony that's come out today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Phil Weiner. I work with the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm going to be asking you some questions today. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were talking about the observation post and you said people didn't generally come there, or something to that extent. Isn't it true that regular meetings were held at that observation post throughout the time that that was being used in Vukovar? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please be so kind as to repeat your question slowly. It was really too much at a time. Could you kindly repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that meetings were regularly held at that observation post while it was being used in that manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that one of the rooms in that building, on that complex, was a meeting room? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit 794, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you could first look and see this 5 that's in a circle that's up on the right. Do you see that, sir, on the -- is that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise this sketch? This sketch was drawn by Captain Radic; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand you. What does this sketch mean? Oh, is it "sketch" in the sense of a drawing, a sketch of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware that Captain Radic has drawn that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I see the drawing or the sketch, but I don't know who drew it. But you said something a few moments ago, and I said at the very outset of my testimony that this was the company working office, not a meeting room. These are two different concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Are you aware that Captain Radic drew that sketch; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: I see the sketch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could they move the sketch down a little bit, please, so you can see the bottom -- actually, I have copies of that. One second, please. Let me get it. This is in B/C/S. Here is the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you see that room, number 5, that you testified was where Captain Radic used to sit and work? Do you see that at the top, sir? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And now could we move down to the bottom where they have the explanations of what that number 5 is. Could we move over a little bit? Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And let's see how Captain Radic described that room. "Old house room for meetings." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is written here. But was this drawn by Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it was, sir. That's what your captain said, that it was used for meetings. Will you now accept that that house was used for meetings, or that room in that house was used for meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: That was the company office. Here it says "room for my meetings in the old house." I can believe it and I cannot believe it. In view of the way I was treated by your gentleman in Belgrade, I cannot claim that it was written by Captain Radic. But that it was the company office, yes. Yes. The company office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you would like, we have a 52-minute plus -- approximately 50-second video of that meeting in Belgrade. It was all videoed. We can play that, and if you have any complaints, you can happily make them. We would be happy to play that for you, and I think we'll see that you're not telling the truth about that either. Sir, isn't it true that meetings were held in that room? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: As for the duration, I came here to tell the truth and nothing but the truth. That is the company office. What is written here is "room for my meetings in the old house." That is the old house by the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And meetings were held is there; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2D4
utterances.text: If Captain Radic calls me to tell me what my assignments are, to spell out precisely how much ammunition should be requested, so on and so forth, you can understand that as a meeting room then. But, in principle, there can be no meeting room; there can only be an office, a working office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
